subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 10 periods = 450 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 7h 30min

periods.activity_title: Reading the Story Aloud: Seed to Sapling

time_bands.activity: Activate prior knowledge with a brief oral exchange: ask students whether they have ever planted something and watched it grow. Invite two or three responses to build an imaginative foothold before the story opens.

Teacher reads the story aloud (pp. 155–164, Part I and the opening of Part II) at a measured pace, with students following in their textbooks. Pause briefly at the goat episode and the grass-cutter episode to let the mood settle before continuing.
Invite students to share in one sentence what image from the reading stayed with them most vividly. Collect three or four responses as a light comprehension check before closing.

periods.teacher_notes: The story's power rests in its quietly accumulating detail — the seasons, the setbacks, the recoveries. Read at a pace that lets each obstacle land before moving on. Students may struggle to locate Mussoorie on a mental map; a brief orienting comment about the Himalayan foothills will help.

periods.activity_title: Reading Continues: Blossoms, Guests, and a Final Question

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.159): arrange story events in correct order — oral sharing.

time_bands.activity: Continue shared reading of Part II from the blossoms onwards through to the story's final lines (pp. 164–165), with students taking turns reading paragraphs aloud while classmates follow silently. Pause at Rakesh's closing whisper for brief whole-class reflection.

Students work on the event-sequencing task from "Let us discuss" (p.159), arranging the ten listed events in story order individually, then comparing with a partner. Call on pairs to share their final sequence.

Consolidate by asking: which two events in the sequence show the tree was resilient rather than fragile? Take responses and connect them to the grandfather's earlier assurance that cherry trees are tough.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read Part I aloud together, students bring a sense of the story's arc into this reading of Part II. The sequencing task is the primary comprehension check here; watch for students who place Rakesh's birthday scene too early — the birthday marks his ninth year, which is near the story's end. Students uncertain about sequencing benefit from being asked to find a page reference for each event before deciding its place.

periods.activity_title: Cause and Effect: The Tree's Trials and Recoveries

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.164): complete cause-and-effect table for Part II — pair share.
Let us think and reflect (p.166): answer factual and inferential comprehension questions — class discussion.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.159): write two to three sentences on whether the cherry tree would survive and why.

time_bands.activity: Students complete the cause-and-effect table from "Let us think and reflect" (p.164) in pairs, filling in the missing causes and effects for events in Part II. Select three pairs to share contrasting responses and build the completed table together on the board.

Open the comprehension questions from "Let us think and reflect" (p.166) as a whole-class discussion. Focus on: why Rakesh was sent to Mussoorie, how life in the Himalayan foothills is described, and the relationship between Rakesh and his grandfather. Encourage students to cite specific lines or details.

Pose the closing question as an open reflective prompt: why did grandfather answer "We planted it ourselves" rather than naming the tree's beauty? Accept two or three responses and leave the question gently open.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the full story together, students are now ready to examine how setbacks — the goat, the scythe, the snow — function structurally as paired events (harm followed by recovery). The cause-and-effect table makes this visible. For the comprehension questions, prioritise the inferential items (the relationship between Rakesh and grandfather, life in the foothills) over the purely factual ones, as these yield richer discussion.

periods.activity_title: Close Reading: Two Extracts, Two Voices

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.165): extract 1 questions — the grandfather's advice on luck and effort.
Let us think and reflect (p.165–166): extract 2 questions — winter hardship and birthday parallel.

time_bands.activity: Invite students to locate Extract 1 (p.165) in their textbooks and read it silently. Draw attention to the dialogue's rhythm — the rapid exchange between Rakesh and grandfather — before opening the questions.

Work through the Extract 1 questions (p.165) together: the phrase-substitution item, the inference about Rakesh rolling the seed, the sentence-completion on what planting shows, and the short answer on grandfather's view of luck. Students write answers individually, then compare with a partner.

Move to Extract 2 (p.165–166). Students read aloud then tackle the four questions: the inference about field-mice seeking shelter, the tree-bending inference item, grandfather's mood during early winter, and the symbolic sentence-completion comparing Rakesh's age to the tree's. Discuss responses as a class.

Consolidate by asking: both extracts are brief but reveal a great deal about a character. Which single word or phrase in each extract carries the most meaning? Accept two or three responses and note them on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Having discussed the story's shape and its factual events, students are now working at the level of word choice and inference. A common difficulty in close-reading tasks is conflating what is stated with what is implied — students may copy a phrase rather than interpret it. For the Extract 2 weather questions, remind students that the narrator uses the physical environment as a mirror for mood, a technique they can name once they see it in action.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Voices for Trees: Chipko to Jadav Payeng

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.170): listen and identify four true statements from seven — class check.

time_bands.activity: Before playing the transcript, tell students they will hear a conversation between a son and his mother about environmental movements and individuals. Ask them to keep a blank page ready to note down names and key facts as they listen.

Read the transcript aloud (p.201) at natural conversation pace, giving each voice a distinct tone. Students listen and note what they catch about the Chipko Movement, the Appiko Movement, Saalumarada Thimakka, and Jadav Payeng.

Read the seven statements from the "Let us listen" task (p.170) aloud, one by one. Students mark T or F for each, then compare with a neighbour before the class decides the four true statements together.
Play a second read of the transcript, slower, while students check and correct their answers. Open a brief class review of any contested statements, citing the transcript line that resolves them.
Close with a one-minute reflection: which person or movement from the transcript connects most closely to Rakesh's experience of growing the cherry tree, and why? Take two or three responses.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript is self-contained: the son and mother cover four environmental topics in sequence, and each is testable on its own. Students often confuse Saalumarada Thimakka (who planted trees since 1948) with Jadav Payeng (who converted barren land over thirty years) — listen for this error during the class review and address it with a direct reference to the transcript. Statement 4 versus Statement 5 is a fine distinction (the mother's desire to share versus her curiosity to hear); making that distinction explicit sharpens critical listening.

periods.activity_title: Syllables Aloud, Then Speaking on Van Mahotsav

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.166–167): read words aloud, mark syllables, check beats in pairs.
Let us speak (p.167–168): prepare and deliver a short spoken piece on Van Mahotsav Diwas.

time_bands.activity: Pairs read the eleven words from the syllable task (pp. 166–167) aloud: mountains, grandfather, tender, disturbed, caterpillar, Himalayan, performed, intention, slope, newspaper, favourite. Each pair writes the syllable count, then reads again clapping the beats. Pairs compare counts with adjacent pairs before a class check.

Introduce the Van Mahotsav Diwas speaking task (pp. 167–168). Give students a preparation window: they jot brief notes under the five given prompts — when, who, why, how, message. Circulate to support students building their spoken structure.

Four to five students deliver their short spoken pieces to the class. Peers listen and note one thing they found clear and one question the speaker left unanswered. The teacher offers brief spoken feedback after each delivery.

Close with a whole-class check: which of the five speaking prompts proved hardest to address and why? Surface two or three responses to consolidate what made the topic challenging to speak about fluently.

periods.teacher_notes: The syllable activity is a warm-up that also builds confident articulation before the longer speaking task. Students sometimes prepare notes and then read them aloud rather than speaking naturally — a brief reminder that notes are a scaffold, not a script, helps. The Van Mahotsav topic connects directly to the story's celebration of planting; students who recall Rakesh's act of planting will find the thematic link natural.

periods.activity_title: Completing a Magazine Article: Trees — Our Lifeline

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.171–172): complete the gapped magazine article using the given word-and-phrase box — individual then class check.

time_bands.activity: Read the complete article text aloud with the gaps spoken as "blank", so students hear the full flow before working on individual items. Ask students to identify which gaps are likely to carry a connector word and which carry a content phrase — this metacognitive framing supports better selection.

Students work individually to fill in all ten blanks (pp. 171–172) from the word-and-phrase box. Encourage re-reading the completed sentence before moving to the next blank. Students who finish early read their completed article silently to check for logical coherence.

Whole-class check: call on individual students to read their answer for each blank in sequence, building the complete article on the board or reading it aloud. Discuss any blanks where more than one word from the box seemed plausible.

Ask students to look at the completed article and identify the overall structure — opening claim, body reasons, hypothetical paragraph, conclusion. Naming the structure helps them recognise the pattern as a reusable form.

periods.teacher_notes: The task uses a closed word-and-phrase bank, which makes it highly guided — the challenge lies in selecting the right connector or phrase for the logical flow of each sentence, not in generating language freely. Blanks (v) and (vii) in particular require students to distinguish "Moreover" (addition) from "If trees were not there" (condition); confusion between these reflects a weak grasp of discourse connectors rather than vocabulary knowledge. The article's environmental theme echoes the story's central preoccupation with nurturing living things.

periods.activity_title: Word Families, Taste Words, Antonyms, and Tense in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.166): identify the odd word in each set — paired reasoning, class check.
Let us learn (p.167): match taste words to food items and write sentences — individual work.
Let us learn (p.167): choose correct antonyms from the box for eight given words.

time_bands.activity: Odd-word task (p.166): display each of the four word sets in turn. Pairs discuss which word does not belong and — crucially — why the other three form a set. Share reasoning with the class; establish that the criterion must be semantic, not alphabetical or length-based.

Taste-words task (p.167): students independently match the seven taste words to the food items, then use any five taste words in original sentences of their own. Circulate to check that sentences are not simply "Tamarind is tangy" — encourage students to embed the word in a context or comparison.

Antonyms task (p.167): students select the correct antonym from the box for each of the eight given words, then justify two choices aloud. Draw attention to the two extra words and ask what makes them unsuitable.

Quick consolidation: ask which word from the odd-word, taste-word, or antonym sets appeared in the story itself. Students scan briefly and name examples — connecting new vocabulary to the text they have already read.

periods.teacher_notes: Three vocabulary tasks in sequence run the risk of feeling mechanical. Keep the odd-word discussion genuinely open — there can be more than one defensible answer if students articulate clear criteria, and accepting a well-argued alternative builds metalinguistic confidence. The taste-word sentences are an opportunity for playful, personal language; resist correcting creative choices unless grammar is broken. Note that the tense-identification and tense-practice tasks are held for a dedicated grammar focus in the next sitting.

periods.activity_title: Past Tenses in Action and Exploring Indian Environmentalists

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.167): identify and name tense forms in three story sentences — class analysis.
Let us learn (p.168): fill blanks with correct past tense forms in the grandparents passage.
Let us explore (p.172): find and share information about Indian environmentalists — paired research notes.

time_bands.activity: Display the three sentences from the tense-identification task (p.167) on the board. Students underline verbs individually, then classify each as simple past, past progressive, or past perfect. Discuss each sentence as a class, establishing why the chosen form fits its context.

Students complete the ten-blank cloze passage (p.168) individually, selecting simple past, past progressive, or past perfect as required by context. Pairs compare answers and resolve differences before a whole-class review of the most contested blanks.

In pairs, students read the brief profile of Kailash Sankhala from "Let us explore" (p.172) and use available reference materials or prior knowledge to gather two or three facts about one other Indian environmentalist. Each pair prepares three key points to share orally with the class.

Four pairs share their environmentalist profiles in under a minute each. After each share, the class identifies one connection — however slight — between that person's work and the themes of patience and nurturing in the story.

periods.teacher_notes: The tense work is anchored in sentences drawn directly from the story, so the grammar remains textually grounded. The trickiest item in the cloze passage is blank (iv) — "had imparted" requires students to see the past-perfect marking of an action completed before another past event. For the beyond-text research, the Chipko Movement figures from the listening conversation (Saalumarada Thimakka, Jadav Payeng) are readily available starting points if students need a direction.
materials: Reference books or printed fact-sheets on Indian environmentalists

periods.activity_title: The Whole Story: Weaving Together Language, Nature, and Meaning

time_bands.activity: Open with a whole-class discussion: across the story, the grammar, the listening conversation, and the speaking topics, one idea returns — that patient, deliberate effort transforms something small into something significant. Ask students to name three examples from the chapter where this is true, drawing from any part of the work they know.

Present three short paired comparisons for small-group discussion: (1) how Rakesh's relationship with nature compares with Jadav Payeng's as described in the listening conversation; (2) how the antonyms "tender" and "sturdy" both describe the cherry tree at different points; (3) how the article structure in the writing task (opening claim, body, hypothetical, conclusion) mirrors the story's structure. Groups spend roughly three minutes on each and then share one insight.

Students write independently for eight to ten minutes: a short personal response (five to seven sentences) to the closing question Rakesh asks — "Is this what it feels to be God?" — drawing on what planting, growing, and caring for something reveals about the relationship between humans and the natural world. Students begin and complete the piece within this band.

Three or four volunteers read their written responses aloud. After each reading, one peer names the most striking idea and one peer names a word or phrase the writer used particularly well. The teacher notes recurring ideas on the board without ranking them.

Close by returning to the story's final image — grandfather in the cane chair, Rakesh beneath the tree, the forest filling with sound — and invite students to name, in a single word, what that image gives them. Collect the words on the board as a collective vocabulary of response, and leave them visible.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws on the story's content, the environmental voices from the listening conversation, the vocabulary of growth and patience, and the writing task's ecological argument — not on any particular activity a class may or may not have done. Any class arriving here equipped only with the story's content can engage with the discussion and the writing task. The personal response writing begins and ends within this sitting; it is not a continuation of any earlier draft.

items.source_context: Rakesh growing cherry tree: seed planting, seasonal setbacks, blossoms, final question to grandfather.
items.item_stem:
Read the four events from The Cherry Tree listed below. Choose the option that gives their correct order of occurrence in the story.
(1) A grass-cutter's scythe cut the cherry tree in two.
(2) Rakesh pressed a cherry seed into the soft soil of the garden.
(3) Grandfather spotted the first pale pink blossom on the tree.
(4) A goat entered the garden and stripped all the leaves from the young tree.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses the order of the goat episode and the grass-cutter episode; both involve damage to the tree but the goat comes first in the monsoon season.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student places the goat episode before the planting of the seed, misreading the story's chronology entirely.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student places the grass-cutter episode at the very start, before the seed is planted, suggesting a misread of Part I.

items.source_lo: Student sequences and interprets narrative events using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Rakesh growing cherry tree: seed planting, seasonal setbacks, blossoms, final question to grandfather.
items.item_stem: Near the end of the story, when Rakesh asks his grandfather why the cherry tree is special among all the trees around them, grandfather replies simply, "We planted it ourselves." What does this reply reveal about what grandfather believes gives something its true value? Use evidence from the story to support your answer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Grandfather's reply suggests he believes that personal effort and care — not mere natural existence — give something its deepest meaning; because Rakesh and he planted the seed, watered it, and watched it through setbacks, the tree carries the history of their shared attention in a way no wild tree can match.

items.source_lo: Student identifies key information and distinctions from a spoken conversation using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Conversation about Chipko Movement, Appiko Movement, Saalumarada Thimakka, and Jadav Payeng.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the conversation between the son and his mother. Then read each statement below and write True or False.
1. The son told his mother he was making a PowerPoint presentation about the Chipko Movement.
2. According to the mother, the Appiko Movement involved only planting new trees, not protecting existing ones.
3. The son described Saalumarada Thimakka as an Indian environmentalist who has been planting trees since 1948.
4. The mother said that Jadav Payeng transformed a barren land into a forest in under ten years.

options.text: According to the mother, the Appiko Movement involved only planting new trees, not protecting existing ones.
The mother said that Jadav Payeng transformed a barren land into a forest in under ten years.
The son described Saalumarada Thimakka as an Indian environmentalist who has been planting trees since 1948.
The son told his mother he was making a PowerPoint presentation about the Chipko Movement.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the son explicitly says he has to make a PowerPoint presentation and talk about the Chipko Movement in class.
2. False — the mother says people in the Appiko Movement hugged trees to protect them AND also regenerated forest areas in the Western Ghats, so protection and regeneration both featured.
3. True — the son states Saalumarada Thimakka has been planting trees since 1948.
4. False — the mother says it took Jadav Payeng thirty years to achieve this, not under ten years.

items.source_lo: Student identifies key information and distinctions from a spoken conversation using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Conversation about Chipko Movement, Appiko Movement, Saalumarada Thimakka, and Jadav Payeng.
items.item_stem: In the conversation, the son says he admires Saalumarada Thimakka for "the commitment she has towards conserving the environment." Based on what the son says about Jadav Payeng in the same conversation, explain in two or three sentences what quality the son most admires in Payeng, and whether this quality is similar to or different from what he admires in Thimakka.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The son admires Jadav Payeng for his extraordinary perseverance — single-handedly planting nearly forty million trees over thirty years to transform barren land into a lush forest. This is very similar to his admiration for Thimakka: both figures demonstrate sustained, long-term personal commitment to the environment rather than a single dramatic act.

items.item_stem: Van Mahotsav is a week-long tree-planting festival celebrated across India each July. Speak for about two minutes on why Van Mahotsav matters today, using at least two specific reasons and giving your own view on what message it sends to young people. You may refer to ideas from the story of Rakesh and his cherry tree if you wish.

expected_elements: States at least two reasons why Van Mahotsav is relevant.
Expresses a personal opinion with a supporting reason.
Maintains a clear spoken structure: opening, body, closing thought.
Uses appropriate vocabulary — environmental or story-related terms welcome.

items.item_stem:
Below is a short paragraph from a draft article about trees. Five words or phrases are missing. Choose the most suitable word or phrase for each blank from the box given.

Box: absorb carbon dioxide, Additionally, reduces pollution, To conclude, would stop existing

Trees are among the most important living things on our planet. Without them, life as we know it __(i)__. Trees __(ii)__ and release oxygen, helping us breathe clean air. This process also __(iii)__ and keeps the environment healthy. __(iv)__, trees provide food, shelter, and habitat for countless animals and birds. __(v)__, it is clear that protecting trees is not a choice but a necessity.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (i) would stop existing; (ii) absorb carbon dioxide; (iii) reduces pollution; (iv) Additionally; (v) To conclude.

items.item_stem: A school magazine has invited students to write a short opinion piece (about 80–100 words) on the following question: "Should every student be required to plant and care for at least one tree during their school years?" Write your opinion piece. Give at least two reasons to support your view, and end with a clear concluding statement.

expected_elements: States a clear opinion in the opening sentence.
Provides at least two distinct reasons with brief explanations.
Uses one or two discourse connectors (Moreover, Additionally, Therefore).
Closes with a concluding statement that restates or extends the opinion.

items.item_stem:
The following sentences are inspired by events in The Cherry Tree. Fill in each blank with the correct past tense form of the verb in brackets — simple past, past progressive, or past perfect — as required by the context.

(i) When the goat entered the garden, Rakesh ______________ (water) the cherry tree nearby.
(ii) By the time February arrived, the cherry tree ______________ (survive) three harsh seasons.
(iii) Grandfather ______________ (spot) the first pale blossom early one morning and called out in delight.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (i) was watering (past progressive — an action in progress when interrupted); (ii) had survived (past perfect — completed before another past event); (iii) spotted (simple past — completed action at a specific moment).

items.item_stem: Read the profile of Kailash Sankhala in "Let us explore" (p.172). Then write a response (four to five sentences) in which you explain: (a) what environmental problem Sankhala's work addressed, and (b) why counting or studying a species can be the first step in protecting it. Use your own words.

expected_elements: Identifies the threat of tiger extinction as Sankhala's concern.
Notes his census work and appointment as first director of Project Tiger.
Explains that data on a species reveals how endangered it is.
Connects evidence-based knowledge to targeted conservation action.
Written in student's own words, not copied from the profile.

items.source_context: Famous banyan trees of India; Indian environmentalists including Kailash Sankhala, Saalumarada Thimakka, Jadav Payeng.
items.item_stem: Project: Choose one Indian environmentalist — from those mentioned in this chapter or from your own reading — who worked to protect or restore a specific part of the natural world. Research their work and prepare a brief illustrated profile (one page) that covers: (1) the environmental problem they tackled, (2) the method or approach they used, (3) the change they brought about, and (4) what you find most inspiring about their work. Be ready to present your profile to the class.

expected_elements: Names a specific environmentalist and the problem they addressed.
Describes their method with at least one concrete detail.
States a measurable or observable outcome of their work.
Offers a personal reflection connecting the figure's effort to wider environmental values.
